claim: Twenty-five volunteers (15 females, mean age 26 years, range 22–34 years) participated in the MEG experiment.
source: Twenty-five volunteers (15 females, mean age 26 years, range 22–34 years) participated in the MEG experiment, approved by the Institutional Review Board of the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (protocol #14N-0002).
evidence: Direct statement of participant demographics in the Methods section.

claim: One participant did not complete the MEG experiment due to discomfort and was removed from further procedures, leaving 24 participants in the MEG dataset.
source: One participant did not complete the MEG experiment due to discomfort and was removed from further procedures, leaving 24 participants in the MEG dataset.
evidence: Direct statement about participant exclusion in the Methods section.

claim: A total of 38 volunteers (26 females, mean age 27 years, range 20–38 years) participated in the fMRI experiment.
source: A total of 38 volunteers (26 females, mean age 27 years, range 20–38 years) participated in the fMRI experiment, following the study protocol (s15-01323) approved by the Institutional Board Review of New York University School of Medicine.
evidence: Direct statement of participant demographics in the Methods section.

claim: Ten volunteers were excluded from the fMRI experiment due to not completing the task and three were removed from data analysis due to poor behavioral performance, leaving 25 volunteers in the fMRI dataset.
source: Ten volunteers were excluded due to not completing the task and three were removed from data analysis due to poor behavioral performance, leaving 25 volunteers in the fMRI dataset.
evidence: Direct statement about participant exclusion in the Methods section.

claim: MEG participants reported 44.9±3.6% of the images as recognized.
source: MEG participants reported 44.9±3.6% of the images as recognized (mean ± SEM, W=105, p = 0.21, two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test against 50%)
evidence: Quantitative behavioral result with statistical test reported in the Results section.

claim: The mean recognition rate in fMRI participants was 48.0±2.6%.
source: the mean recognition rate in fMRI participants was 48.0±2.6% (W=126.5, p=0.34, Figure 1C)
evidence: Quantitative behavioral result with statistical test reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Recognition rates in both MEG and fMRI experiments did not differ from the intended rate of 50%.
source: In both experiments, the recognition rates for real images did not differ from the intended rate of 50%: MEG participants reported 44.9±3.6% of the images as recognized (mean ± SEM, W=105, p = 0.21, two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test against 50%), and the mean recognition rate in fMRI participants was 48.0±2.6% (W=126.5, p=0.34, Figure 1C).
evidence: Statistical comparison to intended threshold with non-significant results.

claim: Object categorization behavior for recognized images was highly accurate across both experiments (MEG: 86.1±1.9%, fMRI: 78.8±2.2%).
source: Further, the object categorization behavior for recognized images was highly accurate across both experiments (MEG: 86.1±1.9%, W=300, p=5.96×10–8; fMRI: 78.8±2.2%, W=325, p=2.9×10–8; one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test against chance level of 25%)
evidence: Quantitative behavioral results with statistical tests showing above-chance performance.

claim: Categorization accuracy for recognized images was significantly higher than those for unrecognized images in both MEG and fMRI experiments.
source: the object categorization behavior for recognized images was highly accurate across both experiments (MEG: 86.1±1.9%, W=300, p=5.96×10–8; fMRI: 78.8±2.2%, W=325, p=2.9×10–8; one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test against chance level of 25%) and significantly higher than those for unrecognized images (MEG: W=300, p=5.96×10–8; fMRI: W=325, p=2.9×10–8; one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 1D).
evidence: Statistical comparison between recognized and unrecognized conditions showing significant difference.

claim: Categorization accuracy in unrecognized trials remained above-chance level (MEG: 40.1±1.8%, fMRI: 32±1.9%).
source: Interestingly, categorization accuracy in unrecognized trials remained above-chance level (MEG: 40.1±1.8%, W=300, p=5.96×10–8; fMRI: 32±1.9%, W=251, p=0.002)
evidence: Quantitative behavioral results with statistical tests showing above-chance performance.

claim: Above-chance discrimination performance in conditions where the stimulus content did not reach awareness is consistent with previous studies.
source: categorization accuracy in unrecognized trials remained above-chance level (MEG: 40.1±1.8%, W=300, p=5.96×10–8; fMRI: 32±1.9%, W=251, p=0.002), consistent with previous studies showing above-chance discrimination performance in conditions where the stimulus content did not reach awareness (Lau and Passingham, 2006; Hesselmann et al., 2011; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: Reference to prior literature supporting the observed finding.

claim: Recognition outcome could be significantly decoded from 200 to 900 ms after stimulus onset.
source: Recognition outcome could be significantly decoded from 200 to 900 ms after stimulus onset (p<0.05, cluster-based permutation test, Figure 2A)
evidence: Decoding analysis result with statistical significance and time window specified.

claim: Peak decoding of recognition outcome occurred at 580 ms.
source: Recognition outcome could be significantly decoded from 200 to 900 ms after stimulus onset (p<0.05, cluster-based permutation test, Figure 2A), with peak decoding at 580 ms.
evidence: Specific timing of peak decoding accuracy reported.

claim: The decodability of image category was highly dependent on subjective recognition.
source: Similar to previous fMRI findings (Levinson et al., 2021), the decodability of image category was highly dependent on subjective recognition (Figure 2B).
evidence: Comparison to prior findings and reference to figure showing differential decodability.

claim: When images were reported as unrecognized, image category was undecodable throughout the epoch.
source: When images were reported as unrecognized, image category was undecodable throughout the epoch (Figure 2B, red).
evidence: Decoding analysis result showing lack of category information in unrecognized trials.

claim: When images were recognized, decoding accuracy for category membership peaked at 290 ms the first time, though it did not survive cluster correction.
source: By contrast, when the same identical images were recognized, decoding accuracy for category membership peaked at 290 ms the first time, though it did not survive cluster correction
evidence: Decoding analysis result with timing information and statistical qualification.

claim: Category decoding accuracy reached significance at 470 ms and remained significant until 1060 ms in recognized trials.
source: decoding accuracy reached significance at 470 ms and remained significant until 1060 ms (Figure 2B, green).
evidence: Decoding analysis result with specific time window of significance.

claim: The results reveal long-lasting neural processes elicited by brief stimuli.
source: These results reveal long-lasting neural processes elicited by brief stimuli, consistent with earlier studies using threshold-level visual stimuli (Dehaene and Changeux, 2011; Li et al., 2014; Baria et al., 2017).
evidence: Interpretation of results with reference to prior literature.

claim: There is a rise of stimulus-evoked neural processes influencing recognition behavior at ~200 ms, preceding the emergence of category information at ~470 ms.
source: At the same time, they reveal a rise of stimulus-evoked neural processes influencing recognition behavior at ~200 ms, preceding the emergence of category information at ~470 ms.
evidence: Temporal sequence of neural processes inferred from decoding results.

claim: When image visibility was high, there was a fast rise of category information within the first 200 ms after stimulus onset (reaching significance at 110 ms, peaking at 170 ms).
source: Consistent with earlier studies, we found that when image visibility was high, there was a fast rise of category information within the first 200 ms after stimulus onset (reaching significance at 110 ms, peaking at 170 ms; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Decoding analysis result from localizer task with high-contrast images.

claim: The late onset of category information observed in the main task was due to the more challenging viewing condition.
source: This result confirms that the late onset of category information observed in the main task was due to the more challenging viewing condition, likely reflecting the more time-consuming recurrent processing involving corticocortical feedback activity (Lamme and Roelfsema, 2000; Fyall et al., 2017; Kar and DiCarlo, 2021).
evidence: Comparison between high and low visibility conditions with interpretation based on prior literature.

claim: The mean dissimilarity between recognized images was significantly lower than between unrecognized images at most of the post-stimulus time points (130–1900 ms).
source: As shown in Figure 2E, the mean dissimilarity between recognized images (green) was significantly lower than between unrecognized images (red) at most of the post-stimulus time points (130–1900 ms, blue horizontal bar)
evidence: RSA result showing differential clustering between recognized and unrecognized images.

claim: Neural activity associated with recognized images contained sharper category information compared to unrecognized images despite the overall smaller dissimilarities among each other.
source: Together with our report of image category being only decodable in recognized trials but not unrecognized trials (Figure 2B), the strong clustering effect of recognized images indicates that neural activity associated with recognized images contained sharper category information compared to unrecognized images despite the overall smaller dissimilarities among each other.
evidence: Integration of decoding and RSA results to infer representational properties.

claim: Significant category information occurred shortly before ~500 ms and decayed at ~1000 ms in recognized trials.
source: As expected, the result was qualitatively similar to category decoding: Significant category information occurred shortly before ~500 ms and decayed at ~1000 ms in recognized trials, whereas no category information was evident in unrecognized trials (Figure 2F, left).
evidence: RSA-based analysis result showing temporal dynamics of category information.

claim: No category information was evident in unrecognized trials based on RSA analysis.
source: Significant category information occurred shortly before ~500 ms and decayed at ~1000 ms in recognized trials, whereas no category information was evident in unrecognized trials (Figure 2F, left).
evidence: RSA-based analysis result showing lack of category information in unrecognized trials.

claim: Successful recognition is associated with a shrinking representational space occupied by cortical activity at 130 ms.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that successful recognition is associated with a shrinking representational space occupied by cortical activity at 130 ms, which may have a facilitating effect on the formation of object category representation that reaches significance at ~470 ms.
evidence: Integration of RSA results to infer temporal dynamics of representational changes.

claim: The shrinking representational space may have a facilitating effect on the formation of object category representation that reaches significance at ~470 ms.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that successful recognition is associated with a shrinking representational space occupied by cortical activity at 130 ms, which may have a facilitating effect on the formation of object category representation that reaches significance at ~470 ms.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the functional relationship between representational changes and category formation.

claim: The earliest significance onset of recognition model effects was at 110 ms concurrently in multiple VTC, TPN, and DMN regions.
source: The earliest significance onset was at 110 ms concurrently in multiple VTC (face, animal, and house), TPN (bilateral MFG, bilateral IPS, and right IFJ), and DMN (bilateral AG, left SFG) regions, all leading to a transient peak at ~150 ms (Figure 4, blue and Figure 4—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: MEG-fMRI fusion result showing concurrent onset across multiple regions.

claim: Recognition model effects in the VTC predominantly existed in the first 1000 ms but were largely undetectable from 1000 ms onward.
source: In contrast, recognition model-related effects in the VTC predominantly existed in the first 1000 ms but were largely undetectable from 1000 ms onward, and were characterized by a transient, intermittent occurrence (Figure 4A, left; Figure 4B, 'face' ROI; Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: MEG-fMRI fusion result showing temporal dynamics in VTC.

claim: Recognition model-related effects in the EVC became statistically significant at ~600 ms and disappeared by 1000 ms after stimulus onset.
source: Notably, recognition model-related effects in the EVC were late and transient; they became statistically significant at ~600 ms and disappeared by 1000 ms after stimulus onset.
evidence: MEG-fMRI fusion result showing late and transient effects in EVC.

claim: Two-state model-related effects in EVC had the shortest onset latency at 120 ms.
source: For instance, while EVC regions had by far the latest onset time for recognition model effects (600 ms), they were among the ROIs wherein the two-state model-related effects had the shortest onset latency (120 ms, Figure 4B, 'V1'; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: MEG-fMRI fusion result showing early two-state model effects in EVC.

claim: Two-state model-related effects in EVC were sustained within the first second after stimulus onset.
source: Moreover, in stark contrast to the transient nature of recognition model effects in EVC, the two-state model-related effects were sustained within the first second after stimulus onset.
evidence: MEG-fMRI fusion result showing sustained effects in EVC.

claim: Two-state model-related effects showed a more stable temporal dynamic than recognition model-related effects.
source: Overall, two-state model-related effects showed a more stable temporal dynamic than recognition model-related effects.
evidence: Comparison of temporal dynamics between two models across regions.

claim: Both recognition and two-state models are associated with early, concurrent onset of significant processes across widespread ROIs.
source: In sum, both recognition and two-state models are associated with early, concurrent onset of significant processes across widespread ROIs, but the two models capture different aspects of recognition-related processing and are associated with distinct network-level patterns
evidence: Summary of MEG-fMRI fusion results comparing two models.

claim: The two-state model was the superior model for explaining neural dynamics in EVC (F1,799 = 1021.34, p=5.14 × 10–145, η2G=0.32).
source: The two-state model was the superior model for explaining neural dynamics in EVC (F1,799 = 1021.34, p=5.14 × 10–145, η2G=0.32; Figure 5A)
evidence: ANOVA result showing model superiority in EVC.

claim: The two-state model was the superior model for explaining neural dynamics in VTC (F1,799 = 892.66, p=2.79 × 10–132, η2G=0.31).
source: The two-state model was the superior model for explaining neural dynamics in EVC (F1,799 = 1021.34, p=5.14 × 10–145, η2G=0.32; Figure 5A) and VTC (F1,799 = 892.66, p=2.79 × 10–132, η2G=0.31; Figure 5B)
evidence: ANOVA result showing model superiority in VTC.

claim: Recognition model was superior for SAL (F1,799 = 12.33, p=4.72 × 10–4, η2G=0.01).
source: while recognition model was superior for SAL (F1,799 = 12.33, p=4.72 × 10–4, η2G=0.01; Figure 5C)
evidence: ANOVA result showing model superiority in SAL.

claim: Recognition model was superior for DAN (F1,799 = 5104.20, p=0, η2G=0.77).
source: while recognition model was superior for SAL (F1,799 = 12.33, p=4.72 × 10–4, η2G=0.01; Figure 5C), DAN (F1,799 = 5104.20, p=0, η2G=0.77; Figure 5D)
evidence: ANOVA result showing model superiority in DAN.

claim: Recognition model was superior for FPCN (F1,799 = 740.60, p=6.42 × 10–116, η2G=0.36).
source: while recognition model was superior for SAL (F1,799 = 12.33, p=4.72 × 10–4, η2G=0.01; Figure 5C), DAN (F1,799 = 5104.20, p=0, η2G=0.77; Figure 5D), FPCN (F1,799 = 740.60, p=6.42 × 10–116, η2G=0.36; Figure 5E)
evidence: ANOVA result showing model superiority in FPCN.

claim: Recognition model was superior for DMN (F1,799 = 34.89, p=5.17 × 10–9, η2G=0.03).
source: while recognition model was superior for SAL (F1,799 = 12.33, p=4.72 × 10–4, η2G=0.01; Figure 5C), DAN (F1,799 = 5104.20, p=0, η2G=0.77; Figure 5D), FPCN (F1,799 = 740.60, p=6.42 × 10–116, η2G=0.36; Figure 5E), and DMN (F1,799 = 34.89, p=5.17 × 10–9, η2G=0.03; Figure 5F).
evidence: ANOVA result showing model superiority in DMN.

claim: There was a significant interaction effect between model and time window in all networks except DAN.
source: There was a significant interaction effect between model and time window in all networks except DAN.
evidence: ANOVA result showing interaction effects across networks.

claim: In EVC, the significant interaction was driven by a sharp decrease in two-state model's explanatory power over time (F1,799 = 155.62, p=9.27 × 10–33, η2G=0.07).
source: In EVC, the significant interaction was driven by a sharp decrease in two-state model's explanatory power over time (F1,799 = 155.62, p=9.27 × 10–33, η2G=0.07).
evidence: ANOVA result showing temporal dynamics of model effects in EVC.

claim: The interaction effect in DMN manifested as a temporal shift in the dominant model, with the recognition model prevailing in the early time window and the two-state model prevailing in the late time window.
source: Interestingly, this interaction effect manifested as a temporal shift in the dominant model in the DMN, with the recognition model prevailing in the early time window (Figure 5F, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, N=801, W=6944, p=3.66×10–46) and the two-state model prevailing in the late time window (N=800, W=23,937, p=1.56×10–11)
evidence: Statistical comparison showing temporal shift in model dominance in DMN.

claim: The temporal shift in DMN's dominant model suggests a flexible adaption in DMN's functional profile to different stages of object recognition processing.
source: Interestingly, this interaction effect manifested as a temporal shift in the dominant model in the DMN, with the recognition model prevailing in the early time window (Figure 5F, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, N=801, W=6944, p=3.66×10–46) and the two-state model prevailing in the late time window (N=800, W=23,937, p=1.56×10–11), suggesting a flexible adaption in DMN's functional profile to different stages of object recognition processing.
evidence: Interpretation of temporal dynamics in DMN based on statistical results.

claim: Neural dynamics in the EVC and VTC were dominated by the two-state model effects.
source: Together, these results reveal differential recognition-related representational dynamics between ventral visual and frontoparietal regions: Neural dynamics in the EVC and VTC were dominated by the two-state model effects, while the recognition model effects predominated in all other networks.
evidence: Summary of network-level differences in model effects.

claim: Recognition model effects predominated in all networks other than EVC and VTC.
source: Together, these results reveal differential recognition-related representational dynamics between ventral visual and frontoparietal regions: Neural dynamics in the EVC and VTC were dominated by the two-state model effects, while the recognition model effects predominated in all other networks.
evidence: Summary of network-level differences in model effects.

claim: The salience (SAL) network had a relatively small main effect of model compared to other networks.
source: In addition, compared to other networks, the salience (SAL) network had a relatively small main effect of model.
evidence: Comparison of effect sizes across networks.

claim: SAL is situated between ventral visual and frontoparietal regions within the cortical hierarchy.
source: Considering that SAL is situated between ventral visual and frontoparietal regions within the cortical hierarchy (Margulies et al., 2016)
evidence: Reference to prior literature on cortical hierarchy.

claim: The results imply a gradual change in the representational format along the cortical hierarchy.
source: Considering that SAL is situated between ventral visual and frontoparietal regions within the cortical hierarchy (Margulies et al., 2016), these results imply a gradual change in the representational format along the cortical hierarchy, similar to that observed previously in a different visual task (González-García et al., 2018).
evidence: Interpretation of results in context of cortical hierarchy with reference to prior work.

claim: Recognition-related information emerged simultaneously across multiple brain networks at 110 ms.
source: Our results show that recognition-related information emerged simultaneously across multiple brain networks at 110 ms, but the representation format differed significantly between ventral visual and frontoparietal regions.
evidence: Summary of main finding from MEG-fMRI fusion analysis.

claim: Neural activity in visual regions is best captured by a state-switch process whereby recognized and unrecognized trials exhibit distinct activity patterns.
source: While neural activity in visual regions is best captured by a state-switch process whereby recognized and unrecognized trials exhibit distinct activity patterns, neural activity in higher-order frontoparietal networks (including salience, dorsal attention, frontoparietal control, and default mode networks) are best described by a variability reduction process whereby recognized trials occupied a smaller region of the neural state space, yet with sharper representation of image category information (Figure 6).
evidence: Summary of differential representational formats across brain regions.

claim: Neural activity in higher-order frontoparietal networks are best described by a variability reduction process whereby recognized trials occupied a smaller region of the neural state space, yet with sharper representation of image category information.
source: While neural activity in visual regions is best captured by a state-switch process whereby recognized and unrecognized trials exhibit distinct activity patterns, neural activity in higher-order frontoparietal networks (including salience, dorsal attention, frontoparietal control, and default mode networks) are best described by a variability reduction process whereby recognized trials occupied a smaller region of the neural state space, yet with sharper representation of image category information (Figure 6).
evidence: Summary of differential representational formats across brain regions.

claim: The early onset observed in the higher-order frontoparietal regions is in accordance with previous MEG and primate neurophysiology findings.
source: The early onset observed in the higher-order frontoparietal regions is in accordance with previous MEG and primate neurophysiology findings, suggesting long-range recurrent processing between higher-order associative and ventral visual regions at an early stage during object recognition under challenging viewing conditions (Bar et al., 2006; Kar and DiCarlo, 2021; Bellet et al., 2022).
evidence: Comparison to prior literature supporting the finding.

claim: Barbeau et al. showed that face-related signals onset simultaneously in fusiform gyrus and inferior frontal gyrus at 110 ms.
source: For instance, consistent with our results, Barbeau et al. showed that face-related signals onset simultaneously in fusiform gyrus and inferior frontal gyrus at 110 ms.
evidence: Reference to specific prior finding supporting parallel onset.

claim: The simultaneity of onset across regions hints at the possibility of parallel processing of visual inputs across multiple cortical regions.
source: These findings contrast with models positing a simple feedforward processing of visual inputs from primary sensory to high-order associative cortices. Instead, the simultaneity hints at the possibility of parallel processing of visual inputs across multiple cortical regions.
evidence: Interpretation of findings in context of processing models.

claim: The early frontoparietal recognition-related signals are triggered by the fast magnocellular inputs via the dorsal visual stream or projected from the pulvinar or mediodorsal nucleus of the thalamus.
source: For example, it has been suggested that the early frontoparietal recognition-related signals are triggered by the fast magnocellular inputs via the dorsal visual stream or projected from the pulvinar or mediodorsal nucleus of the thalamus (Bullier, 2001; Bar, 2003; Kveraga et al., 2007).
evidence: Reference to prior theoretical proposals about neural pathways.

claim: Recognition-related signals in the ventral visual regions are likely to be triggered by inputs via the parvocellular pathway along the ventral visual stream, which may be facilitated by feedback signals from dorsal stream regions.
source: The recognition-related signals in the ventral visual regions, on the contrary, are likely to be triggered by inputs via the parvocellular pathway along the ventral visual stream, which may be facilitated by feedback signals from dorsal stream regions (Bar et al., 2006).
evidence: Interpretation of results with reference to prior work on visual pathways.

claim: Previous monkey and human work associated a reduced neural variability with cortical engagement in stimulus and task processing.
source: Previous monkey and human work associated a reduced neural variability with cortical engagement in stimulus and task processing (Luczak et al., 2009; Ratcliff et al., 2009; Churchland et al., 2010; He, 2013; He and Zempel, 2013; Schurger et al., 2015; Arazi et al., 2017).
evidence: Reference to prior literature on neural variability.

claim: Successful recognition is linked with enhanced stimulus processing in higher-order frontoparietal regions.
source: In line with this interpretation, our finding of reduced neural variability in higher-order frontoparietal regions during recognized trials suggests that successful recognition is linked with enhanced stimulus processing in these regions (consistent with the emergence of category-level information mentioned above).
evidence: Interpretation of results in context of prior literature on neural variability.

claim: Failed recognition may partially result from limited frontoparietal engagement, at least in the context of challenging viewing conditions.
source: On the other hand, the high neural variability in unrecognized trials suggests that failed recognition may partially result from limited frontoparietal engagement, at least in the context of challenging viewing conditions.
evidence: Interpretation of results regarding unrecognized trials.

claim: The asymmetrical reduction in neural variability explained 80% of total shared variance between fMRI and MEG RDMs in the FPCN in the 0–1000 ms time window.
source: The asymmetrical reduction in neural variability was particularly strong in the FPCN and DAN, explaining 80% and 98.4% of total shared variance between fMRI and MEG RDMs in the 0–1000 ms time window.
evidence: Quantitative result showing explanatory power of recognition model in FPCN.

claim: The asymmetrical reduction in neural variability explained 98.4% of total shared variance between fMRI and MEG RDMs in the DAN in the 0–1000 ms time window.
source: The asymmetrical reduction in neural variability was particularly strong in the FPCN and DAN, explaining 80% and 98.4% of total shared variance between fMRI and MEG RDMs in the 0–1000 ms time window.
evidence: Quantitative result showing explanatory power of recognition model in DAN.

claim: FPCN and DAN areas are sources of attentional and executive control.
source: These areas are sources of attentional and executive control (Miller and Cohen, 2001; Corbetta and Shulman, 2002; Duncan, 2010; Ptak, 2012; Buschman and Kastner, 2015).
evidence: Reference to prior literature on functional roles of brain networks.

claim: The enhanced FCPN and DAN engagement during recognized trials may reflect attention-related modulations that support object recognition.
source: Accordingly, it is possible that the enhanced FCPN and DAN engagement during recognized trials reflect attention-related modulations that support object recognition (Serences et al., 2004; Baldauf and Desimone, 2014).
evidence: Speculative interpretation with reference to prior work on attention.

claim: FCPN and DAN regions are actively involved in object recognition processing.
source: In light of the increasing evidence that FCPN and DAN regions are actively involved in object recognition processing (Konen and Kastner, 2008; Freud et al., 2017; Levinson et al., 2021; Ayzenberg and Behrmann, 2022; Mei et al., 2022)
evidence: Reference to accumulating evidence from multiple studies.

claim: The enhanced FCPN and DAN engagement may be directly related to perceptual processing per se.
source: In light of the increasing evidence that FCPN and DAN regions are actively involved in object recognition processing (Konen and Kastner, 2008; Freud et al., 2017; Levinson et al., 2021; Ayzenberg and Behrmann, 2022; Mei et al., 2022), the enhanced FCPN and DAN engagement may be directly related to perceptual processing per se.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on recent literature.

claim: The early recognition-related responses in the FPCN and DAN may reflect an initial, fast analysis of noisy visual input in the dorsal visual stream which facilitates fine-grained analysis happening in the ventral stream.
source: For example, the early recognition-related responses in the FPCN and DAN may reflect an initial, fast analysis of noisy visual input in the dorsal visual stream which facilitates fine-grained analysis happening in the ventral stream (Bullier, 2001; Bar, 2003; Bar et al., 2006).
evidence: Speculative interpretation with reference to prior theoretical work.

claim: Early recognition-related responses in FPCN and DAN may reflect the accumulation of sensory evidence preceding the rise of a particular perceptual experience.
source: Alternatively, they may reflect the accumulation of sensory evidence preceding the rise of a particular perceptual experience (Gold and Shadlen, 2007; Kelly and O'Connell, 2015).
evidence: Alternative speculative interpretation with reference to prior work.

claim: The onset of recognition-related activity according to both models (significance at 110–120 ms) is earlier than the onset of category-level information (initial peak at 290 ms, significance at 470 ms).
source: These interpretations are not mutually exclusive and consistent with our empirical finding that the onset of recognition-related activity according to both models (significance at 110–120 ms) is earlier than the onset of category-level information (initial peak at 290 ms, significance at 470 ms).
evidence: Temporal comparison of different types of neural signals.

claim: Object category-related information reached significance at 470 ms using whole-brain MEG decoding.
source: Using whole-brain MEG decoding, we found that object category-related information reached significance at 470 ms.
evidence: Summary of decoding result.

claim: Category decoding in prior studies using high-contrast, clear object images typically peaked within the first 200 ms.
source: This is markedly later than those reported in previous studies using high-contrast, clear object images, where category decoding typically peaked within the first 200 ms (DiCarlo et al., 2012; Carlson et al., 2013; Cichy et al., 2014; Isik et al., 2014).
evidence: Comparison to prior literature showing timing differences.

claim: In the localizer task with suprathreshold contrasts, object category decoding reached significance at 110 ms and peaked at 170 ms.
source: In a localizer task (with the same image set as used in the main task but presented at suprathreshold contrasts), we found object category decoding reached significance at 110 ms and peaked at 170 ms.
evidence: Control experiment result showing faster category decoding with high-contrast images.

claim: More time-consuming recurrent neural processing is needed for object recognition under high uncertainty/low visibility.
source: These results are consistent with the idea that more time-consuming recurrent neural processing is needed for object recognition under high uncertainty/low visibility.
evidence: Interpretation of timing differences based on stimulus visibility.

claim: The latency for the emergence of object category information increases as the viewing duration becomes shorter.
source: This interpretation is also consistent with recent human electrophysiology findings showing that the latency for the emergence of object category information increases as the viewing duration becomes shorter (Mohsenzadeh et al., 2018)
evidence: Reference to prior findings supporting the interpretation.

claim: The latency for the emergence of object category information increases as the visible part of an object shrinks.
source: This interpretation is also consistent with recent human electrophysiology findings showing that the latency for the emergence of object category information increases as the viewing duration becomes shorter (Mohsenzadeh et al., 2018) or the visible part of an object shrinks (Tang et al., 2018; Rajaei et al., 2019)
evidence: Reference to prior findings supporting the interpretation.

claim: Behavioral responses for the categorization of degraded visual images can be relatively long (up to >1 s).
source: and fits with the relatively long behavioral responses (up to >1 s) for the categorization of degraded visual images (Philiastides and Sajda, 2007; Ratcliff et al., 2009; Hegdé and Kersten, 2010; Philiastides et al., 2011).
evidence: Reference to prior behavioral findings.

claim: DMN regions encoded the content of recognition within its (deactivated) activity patterns despite stronger deactivation in recognized trials.
source: For instance, a previous study using the 7T fMRI dataset investigated herein reported that despite stronger deactivation in recognized trials, DMN regions encoded the content of recognition within its (deactivated) activity patterns (Levinson et al., 2021).
evidence: Reference to prior finding from the same dataset.

claim: Successful recognition is associated with an enhanced DMN engagement despite its deactivation.
source: Here, using stimulus-induced reduction in neural variability as an indicator of cortical engagement, we found that successful recognition is associated with an enhanced DMN engagement despite its deactivation
evidence: Interpretation of results regarding DMN engagement.

claim: Neural activity in the DMN dynamically shifts from recognition model-dominated effects to two-state model-dominated effects.
source: and that neural activity in the DMN dynamically shifts from recognition model-dominated effects (variability reduction in recognized trials) to two-state model-dominated effects (bifurcation between recognized and unrecognized trials).
evidence: Summary of temporal dynamics in DMN.

claim: The shift toward the two-state representational structure in the late stage may indicate an enhanced intercommunication with other areas that were also dominated by the two-state model effects, such as the ventral visual regions.

claim: DMN has a prominent role in both associative processing and prior-guided perception.

claim: The late-stage effect in DMN might reflect interactions between the current visual inputs and the observer's prior knowledge that guide subsequent perceptual decisions and related associations.
source: Speculatively, given DMN's prominent role in both associative processing (Bar et al., 2007; Stawarczyk et al., 2021) and prior-guided perception (González-García et al., 2018; Flounders et al., 2019), this effect might reflect interactions between the current visual inputs and the observer's prior knowledge that guide subsequent perceptual decisions and related associations.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of DMN function in context of prior knowledge.

claim: Under a challenging viewing condition, object recognition-related neural processes emerge early (110–120 ms) and simultaneously across multiple ventral visual and frontoparietal regions despite the late emergence (470 ms) of category-related information.
source: In summary, under a challenging viewing condition, we found that object recognition-related neural processes emerge early (110–120 ms) and simultaneously across multiple ventral visual and frontoparietal regions despite the late emergence (470 ms) of category-related information.
evidence: Summary of main findings.

claim: Brain regions differ in the temporal evolution and representational format of their neural dynamics, in a manner that is roughly organized according to large-scale functional networks.
source: Importantly, brain regions differ in the temporal evolution and representational format of their neural dynamics, in a manner that is roughly organized according to large-scale functional networks.

claim: Object recognition under uncertainty engages a bidirectional coordination between multiple cortical networks with diverse functional roles at an early processing stage.
source: Thus, object recognition under uncertainty engages a bidirectional coordination between multiple cortical networks with diverse functional roles at an early processing stage.

claim: Images were presented for 66.7 ms in both MEG and fMRI experiments.
